name: Chapter 6: Evolution
description: Origin of life, Darwinism, evidences, adaptive radiation, mechanism, Hardy-Weinberg, history of life and human evolution

cards.definition: Study of the history of life forms on earth

cards.term: Why is looking at stars "looking into the past"?
cards.definition: Their light started its journey millions of years ago
About 13.8 billion years

cards.term: Theory explaining the origin of the universe?
cards.definition: Big Bang theory: a singular huge explosion universe expanded and cooled H and He formed gases condensed into galaxies
About 4.5 billion years ago
Water vapour, methane, CO₂, ammonia released from molten mass; no atmosphere initially

cards.term: How did early O₂ and oceans form?
cards.definition:
UV split water
light H₂ escaped
O combined with NH₃ and CH₄ to form water, CO₂
ozone formed
vapour fell as rain to fill depressions
500 million years after earth formed: almost 4 billion years ago
Idea that units of life (spores) were transferred to planets including earth from outer space
Belief that life came from decaying and rotting matter (straw, mud)

cards.term: Who disproved spontaneous generation and how?
cards.definition:
Louis Pasteur:
in pre-sterilised flasks no life arose from killed yeast;
in flasks open to air, organisms arose
→ life comes only from pre-existing life
First life came from pre-existing non-living organic molecules (RNA, protein), preceded by chemical evolution
High temperature, volcanic storms, reducing atmosphere with CH₄, NH₃ etc.
1953, S.L. Miller: electric discharge in a closed flask with CH₄, H₂, NH₃ and water vapour
Formation of amino acids

cards.term: Correction: NCERT prints the gases were "at 8000C". Correct reading?
cards.definition: 800 °C as printed in NCERT (the degree sign was lost); in Miller’s real setup water was boiled (~100 °C) and sparks supplied energy
Sugars, nitrogen bases, pigments and fats

cards.term: Evidence that chemical evolution occurs in space?
cards.definition: Similar compounds found in meteorites

cards.term: When did the first non-cellular life arise?
cards.definition: About 3 billion years ago: giant molecules (RNA, protein, polysaccharides)

cards.term: When did the first cellular life arise (NCERT)?
cards.definition: About 2000 million years ago; single cells in water
Fossil microbes/stromatolites about 3.5 billion years old (NCERT’s 2000 mya is outdated)
First life arose slowly through evolutionary forces from non-living molecules
1) All organisms created as such. 2) Diversity always the same. 3) Earth is about 4000 years old.
H.M.S. Beagle

Living forms share similarities with each other and with extinct forms.
Gradual evolution with extinctions and new forms
Ultimately and only reproductive fitness: fitter individuals leave more progeny
Alfred Wallace, working in the Malay Archipelago

cards.term: Conclusion about earth’s age from Darwinism?
cards.definition: Earth is billions of years old, not thousands
Remains of hard parts of life forms found in rocks
Different-aged rock sediments contain different fossils: life forms varied over time and some are restricted to certain geological spans

cards.term: How is the age of fossils found?
cards.definition: Radioactive dating

cards.term: Living counterparts of dinosaurs in Figure 6.2?
cards.definition: Crocodiles and birds
All vertebrate embryos, incl. human, develop vestigial gill slits behind the head; functional only in fish
Karl Ernst von Baer: embryos never pass through the adult stages of other animals
Ernst Haeckel
Same anatomical structure, different functions result of divergent evolution indicate common ancestry

cards.term: Homologous forelimb bones in whale, bat, cheetah, human?
cards.definition: Humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals, phalanges
Vertebrate hearts and brains
Thorn of Bougainvillea and tendril of Cucurbita
Different structures, same function; result of convergent evolution

Wings of butterfly and bird: Flight, different structure; Eye of octopus and mammal: Vision, different origin; Flippers of penguin and dolphin: Swimming; Sweet potato and potato: Root vs stem modification for storage

cards.definition: HomOlogy = same Origin. AnAlogy = same Activity (function).
Similarities in proteins and genes performing a function in diverse organisms point to common ancestry
If man created new breeds (e.g. dogs) in hundreds of years, nature could do the same over millions of years
Before industrialisation (1850s): more white-winged moths. After (1920): more dark-winged (melanised) moths.

Predators spot moths against a contrasting background.
Soot darkened trunks and killed white lichens, so dark moths were camouflaged
They do not grow in polluted areas
Melanic moth count stayed low where there was no industrialisation

cards.term: Is any variant completely wiped out?
cards.definition: No; only the proportions change

cards.term: Examples of evolution by anthropogenic action?
cards.definition: Resistance to herbicides, pesticides, antibiotics and drugs appearing in months/years

cards.term: Antibiotic resistance explained by Darwinian selection (Exercise 1)?
cards.definition: A few bacteria already carry resistance variations antibiotic kills the rest resistant ones survive and multiply → resistant population
No; it is a stochastic process based on chance events and chance mutation

cards.term: Where did Darwin see his finches?
cards.definition: Galapagos Islands

cards.term: Darwin’s finches: original and derived forms?
cards.definition: From seed-eating ancestors arose insectivorous and vegetarian finches with altered beaks
Evolution of different species in a geographical area starting from a point and radiating to other habitats
Darwin’s finches and Australian marsupials

cards.term: Name marsupials of the Australian radiation (Figure 6.6).
cards.definition:
Tasmanian wolf, tiger cat, banded anteater, marsupial rat, kangaroo,
wombat, bandicoot, koala, marsupial mole, sugar glider

cards.term: When is adaptive radiation called convergent evolution?
cards.definition: When more than one adaptive radiation occurs in an isolated area, giving similar forms

cards.term: Example of convergence: placental vs marsupial?
cards.definition: Placental wolf and Tasmanian wolf (marsupial)

cards.term: Pairs of placental and Australian marsupial mammals (Figure 6.7)?
cards.definition:
Mole–marsupial mole
anteater–numbat
mouse–marsupial mouse
lemur–spotted cuscus
flying squirrel–flying phalanger
bobcat–Tasmanian tiger cat
wolf–Tasmanian wolf

cards.term: Can human evolution be called adaptive radiation? (Exercise 9)
cards.definition: No. It is a single lineage, not many species radiating into different habitats from one ancestor in one area

cards.term: When would natural selection truly have started?
cards.definition: When cellular life with differences in metabolic capability arose

cards.term: Why do microbes evolve faster than fish or fowl?
cards.definition: Rate of new forms is linked to life span; microbes divide in minutes, animals live years

cards.term: Why must fitness have a genetic basis?
cards.definition: Only inherited characteristics can be selected and evolve

cards.term: Two key concepts of Darwinian theory?
cards.definition: Branching descent and natural selection
Evolution driven by use and disuse of organs; acquired characters inherited (giraffe’s neck)
Acquired characters are not inherited; nobody believes the giraffe conjecture any more

cards.term: Who may have influenced Darwin on populations?
cards.definition: Thomas Malthus
Resources limited populations stable members vary most variations inherited theoretical exponential growth → competition

Heritable variations that improve resource use let a few reproduce more.
Over generations the population changes

cards.term: Who proposed mutation theory, and on what plant?
cards.definition: Hugo de Vries, evening primrose

cards.term: De Vries’ mutations vs Darwin’s variations?
cards.definition: Mutations: large, sudden, random, directionless. Darwinian variations: small, directional, gradual.
Single-step large mutation causing speciation (de Vries)

cards.term: What brought clarity between Darwin and de Vries?
cards.definition: Population genetics
Allele frequencies in a population are stable and constant from generation to generation (genetic equilibrium)
Total genes and their alleles in a population

cards.text: Hardy–Weinberg: \( p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1 \), where \( p^2 \) = frequency of {{c1::AA}}, \( 2pq \) = {{c2::Aa}}, \( q^2 \) = {{c3::aa}}.

cards.definition: 1 (sum of all allele frequencies)

cards.term: What indicates evolution in H–W terms?
cards.definition: Measured frequencies differ from expected: disturbance of genetic equilibrium

cards.text: Five factors affecting H–W equilibrium: {{c1::gene migration (gene flow)}}, {{c2::genetic drift}}, {{c3::mutation}}, {{c4::genetic recombination}}, {{c5::natural selection}}.

cards.definition:
Migration of a section of population changes allele frequencies in both populations.
Repeated migration = gene flow
Change in allele frequency by chance
A drifted population so different it becomes a new species; the original drifted group are founders

Hardy–Weinberg

16% of a population is aa. Carrier (Aa) frequency?

Assume equilibrium.
  1. q² = 0.16 → q = 0.4
  2. p = 1 − 0.4 = 0.6
  3. ?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Hardy–Weinberg

16% of a population is aa. Carrier (Aa) frequency?

Assume equilibrium.
  1. q² = 0.16 → q = 0.4
  2. p = 1 − 0.4 = 0.6
  3. 2pq = 2 × 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.48

cards.term: Why is H–W equilibrium rare in nature? (intuition)
cards.definition:
It needs no mutation, no migration, no selection, random mating and a huge population.
Real populations always break at least one
Stabilising: more individuals at mean. Directional: shift away from mean. Disruptive: both extremes favoured.
(a) Stabilising (peak higher, narrower). (b) Directional (peak shifts). (c) Disruptive (two peaks).

cards.term: What did some early cells gain the ability to do?
cards.definition: Release O₂, probably by splitting water like the light reaction
First cellular life: 2000 mya; Invertebrates active: 500 mya; Jawless fish: 350 mya; Sea weeds and few plants: 320 mya; Lobefins move to land: 350 mya; Dinosaurs disappear: 65 mya

cards.definition: About 500 mya (Cambrian–Ordovician); NCERT’s dates are simplified
Plants
Coelacanth (lobefin) off South Africa
The first amphibians; ancestors of frogs and salamanders
Thick-shelled eggs that do not dry up in the sun
Turtles, tortoises, crocodiles
Fell to form coal deposits

cards.term: Fish-like reptiles that returned to water?
cards.definition: Ichthyosaurs (~200 mya)
About 20 feet tall with dagger-like teeth
Birds are living theropod dinosaurs; the non-avian dinosaurs died out ~66 mya, most likely after an asteroid impact

cards.term: What were the first mammals like?
cards.definition: Small, shrew-like
Viviparous (young protected inside mother) and more intelligent in sensing and avoiding danger

cards.term: Why did South American mammals disappear?
cards.definition: Continental drift joined South and North America; North American fauna overrode them

cards.term: Why did Australian pouched mammals survive?
cards.definition: Continental drift isolated them; no competition from other mammals
Whales, dolphins, seals, sea cows

cards.term: Read Figure 6.9: plant groups through geological periods.
cards.definition:
Chlorophyte ancestors
→ tracheophytes, psilophyton
→ bryophytes, lycopods, horsetails, ferns, seed ferns
→ gymnosperms (cycads, conifers)
→ angiosperms (monocots, dicots)

cards.term: Read Figure 6.10: which reptile group gave rise to mammals?
cards.definition: Therapsids (via pelycosaurs/synapsids)
Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus: hairy, walked like gorillas and chimpanzees
Ramapithecus: more man-like. Dryopithecus: more ape-like.

cards.term: Where were man-like fossil bones found?
cards.definition: Ethiopia and Tanzania
Man-like primates in eastern Africa: ≤ 4 feet tall, walked upright
~2 mya in East African grasslands; hunted with stone weapons but ate mainly fruit

Homo habilis: 650–800 cc; first human-like hominid; probably no meat; Homo erectus: ~900 cc; ~1.5 mya; fossils in Java (1891); ate meat; Neanderthal man: 1400 cc; 1,00,000–40,000 yrs ago; hides, buried dead; Homo sapiens: Arose in Africa; modern form during ice age 75,000–10,000 yrs ago

cards.term: When did pre-historic cave art develop?
cards.definition: About 18,000 years ago

cards.term: Indian site of pre-historic cave paintings?
cards.definition: Bhimbetka rock shelter, Raisen district, Madhya Pradesh

cards.term: When did agriculture and settlements begin?
cards.definition: About 10,000 years ago

cards.term: What does Figure 6.11 show about skulls?
cards.definition: The baby chimpanzee skull is more like the adult human skull than the adult chimpanzee skull
Increasing brain size, upright posture, shift to omnivory/meat, tool use, language and self-consciousness
